study.title: Proverbs 14 - Practical wisdom, fear of the LORD, and the contrast between just and perverse
study.overview: The chapter brings together short sayings and strong contrasts to show how wisdom appears in common life: in the home, in speech, in work, in relations, in dealing with the poor, in public justice and in government. The dominant idea is that the conduct aligned with the fear of the Lord produces protection, integrity and life; already madness, lies, violence and arrogance bring ruin, shame and death. The text also insists that appearance and impulse are not good guides: man needs to ponder his steps, avoid evil and act with mercy and prudence.

outline.title: Wisdom in the home, speech and paths
outline.explanation: The first sayings contrast the wise woman and the foolish woman, the righteous and the wicked, the prudent and the scoffer. The chapter shows that wisdom is not abstract: it reveals itself in the administration of the house, in the use of the language and in the ability to discern its own path.

outline.title: Blame, deception and prudence in the face of danger
outline.explanation: Here the blindness of the fool in the face of sin, the danger of the path that seems correct, the instability of the deep-feasure joy and the difference between the naive and the prudent. The emphasis lies on humility, vigilance and refusal of the precipitated anger.

outline.title: Social relations, work and truth
outline.explanation: The passage deals with favoritism, contempt for others, mercy to the humble, diligent work and true witness. Wisdom is presented as a moral force that protects lives and promotes well, while lies and empty discourse impoverish and corrupt.

outline.title: Fear of the Lord, life and just government
outline.explanation: The final section shows that the fear of the LORD generates trust, refuge and life, in contrast to envy, oppression and malice. The chapter ends with justice by raising the peoples and with the king favoring the prudent servant, indicating that wisdom must also mark public life.

study.context: The notes present these proverbs as contrasting moral sentences, of wide application to domestic, social and public life. They do not provide a specific historical scenario for the chapter, but highlight that wisdom is practical and that its consequences appear in daily life, home, work and government.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter presents the fear of the LORD as a structuring principle of wise life. Fearing God is not only inner reverence; it is walking correctly, moving away from evil, speaking with truth, treating the poor with compassion and trusting in God as a refuge. The text also affirms a moral of sowing and harvesting: wisdom builds up, the lie destroys, the precipitated anger produces madness, the ep-rode envy, and justice exalts. In a Protestant evangelical reading, this emphasizes that true piety is not reduced to verbal worship, but shapes character, relations and public responsibilities. Still, the chapter describes sapiential principles, not mechanical promises; it points out real moral tendencies and calls to the right life before God.

scholarViews.insight: The metaphor of the way describes life and conduct; the fear of the LORD is the axis that guides this way of life.
The good wife is a great blessing to the family, because their prudence, piety and diligence make the house prosper.
The fear of the Lord is in full harmony with strong confidence, uniting reverence to God and security in his mercy and goodness.

questions: In what concrete ways do my speech, my work and my household decisions are building or weakening my life around me?
Have I treated the poor, the humble and the neighbor with mercy, or with indifference and contempt?
What signs do I show that I need to exchange impulsiveness, anger or appearance of wisdom for prudence and fear of the LORD?
study.practice: Choose a practical area to obey the chapter this week: talk more truthfully and less quick reaction; examine a habit of work or administration of the house; or exercise concrete mercy to someone in need. Then pray asking that the fear of the LORD rule his footsteps and evaluate, at the end of the week, whether his attitudes brought peace, trust and edification.
study.uncertainty: The scores provided do not identify the historical context of the chapter or explain each verse in detail; therefore, the study is limited to the biblical text and the cited comments. Some poetic expressions of the chapter remain open to interpretive nuances, such as the relationship between wealth and honor, or between trust and fear. Where there is confessional reading, it was presented as an interpretation, not as an indisputable conclusion of the text.
